claims.text: Formation of a single-phase solid solution in noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles under rapid thermal cycling is governed by transient atomic interdiffusion kinetics.
An optimal heating-rate window exists for forming the single-phase solid solution.
The optimal heating-rate window permits sufficient elemental intermixing before phase separation begins.
Outside the optimal heating-rate window, differences in elemental diffusivity cause localized segregation, phase separation, and adverse morphology.
The precursor may initially contain microsegregation or nonuniform local concentration distributions.
Heating rate can be systematically varied while holding overall composition fixed.
The proposed regime assumes elemental diffusivity differences of less than approximately 20%.
Phase selection is mediated by the balance between atomic diffusion rates and transient short-range-order cluster formation.
Transient short-range-order clusters act as nucleation sites.
Excessively rapid heating leaves insufficient time for uniform atomic interdiffusion.
Insufficient interdiffusion produces local composition fluctuations and phase separation.
Optimizing the heating rate gives atoms enough time to overcome local energy barriers and redistribute uniformly.
More uniform atomic redistribution favors a single-phase solid solution over segregated phases and uncontrolled morphologies.
Applying the optimal heating rate will yield more consistent single-phase crystal structures than the baseline rapid-heating process.
Applying the optimal heating rate will improve particle-morphology control relative to baseline.
Applying the optimal heating rate will reduce elemental segregation relative to baseline.
The conventional rapid-heating and cooling baseline frequently produces phase separation, elemental segregation, and uncontrolled particle morphology.
The hypothesis is bounded to noble-metal systems with relatively similar elemental diffusivities and thermal decomposition temperatures, described as within approximately 20% variation.
The applicable processing boundary is rapid thermal cycling with heating durations from sub-second to a few seconds.
